newsitem.title: KUWAIT: UAE closer to announcing $6 billion planes deal.
newsitem.headline: UAE closer to announcing $6 billion planes deal.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates is moving closer to announcing the winner of a $6 billion military aircraft order, military sources said on Monday.
"It could be finalised this year," said a Gulf source familiar with the deal, adding "Don't expect anything before late September, possibly followed by an announcement in October".
UAE talks with European and American warplane makers on a package for up to 80 long-range aircraft have been under way for several years.

U.S. Lockheed Martin Corp's F-16 is pitted against France's Dassault Aviation Rafale and the Eurofighter 2000, made by a consortium of British Aerospace, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA), Spain's CASA and Italy's Alenia Spa.
Sources said an Abu Dhabi committee could meet in September to review final modifications to offers by warplane makers and study financial packages.

Official UAE military sources had earlier told Reuters that Abu Dhabi was now focusing on financial packages which could decide the winner after agreeing with manufacturers on most of the technical requirements.
The UAE's armed forces chief of staff and main arms procurement officer Sheikh Mohammad bin Zaid al-Nahayan recently discussed the order with American and European officials.
The chief of staff's message to them was "the financial package will play a large role in the decision process."

Airforce pilot Sheikh Mohammad, son of UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, flew to Europe on Sunday after three days of talks in Washington where he also discussed other items on Abu Dhabi's long arms shopping list.
A Gulf source said that Sheikh Mohammad brushed away differences with the United States over an air defence system by "placing the requirement on the back burner for the next few years".
Washington has urged Abu Dhabi to drop the Russian S-300 option in favour of Raytheon Co's Patriot "Scud Buster" which gained world fame during the Gulf War.

The U.S. argues that the system is not compatible with mainly Western weaponry deployed in the Gulf, that it could constitute a risk to U.S. warplanes in the area and that it needs larger crews to operate. Kuwait and Riydah both have Patriot systems.
Following Sheikh Mohammad's visit, Congress was notified of a UAE request to buy 72 Sea Sparrow and 24 Harpoon missiles worth $27 million and $90 million respectively.

"This deal sweetner could ease some of the American pressure to finalise the planes order," said an Arab industry executive of the missiles to be deployed on two used Dutch frigates which the UAE bought last year in a $350 million package.
